title: How We Set Math Class up to Fail
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer argues that math class is built around a one-way journey from concrete to abstract, and that this journey asks many students to discard the physical, intuitive knowledge they bring. Using the cone-and-cylinder volume relationship, he contrasts a hands-on popcorn demonstration with the textbook formula problem. He borrows Hayakawa's abstraction ladder and Wendell Johnson's idea of dead-level abstracting to describe teachers who can move up and down between levels as the ones who keep students engaged. A water-sloshing cone problem by Bowman Dickson serves as a model of work along the whole ladder. His conclusion is that math instruction should fortify students' concrete knowledge rather than replace it. A short coda wonders why online videos teach math but rarely teaching.
points: The stated direction of math education, from objects to counts to variables and functions, quietly asks most students to separate themselves from the concrete knowledge they already have.
Teachers who engage students in math share a skill, moving fluidly up and down the ladder of abstraction and preserving the concrete connection while building abstract fluency.
Dead-level abstracting, living on a single rung, is the characteristic failure of math lessons.
A good task like Dickson's cone problem invites both formula use and sensory imagination, so students want to play with it.
Instruction should treat students' concrete knowledge as something to build on, not replace.
quotes: These are two ways of knowing the same thing—one concrete, the other abstract. One you can hold in your hand. The other you can only hold in your head.

There are people in this world who see straight through the corn in the textbook. They look at the problem and don’t think of the kernels you hold in your hand. They see a cone, its diameter, its height, the question, and they know what they’re going to do. These people make up a small percentage of the world’s population and a large percentage of the world’s math professionals.

The same is true of teaching math. But in math class, you’ll often find what Wendell Johnson described as “dead-level abstracting”—people unable to operate at more than one rung of the ladder. They just live there.
